name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
title: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
answer: Threat modelling for legal AI is the practice of identifying what can go wrong when a law firm or in-house team puts a model into a legal workflow, and who or what could cause it. The scope covers the model itself, the data it reads, the tools it calls, the people who prompt it, and the outputs that reach a client or a court. It sits inside AI security audits and enterprise enablement, so the work is usually done before deployment and repeated as the system changes. Because legal work carries privilege, confidentiality and professional duty, the threat list is wider than a typical software review.

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI is the practice of identifying what can go wrong when a law firm or in-house team puts a model into a legal workflow, and who or what could cause it. The scope covers the model itself, the data it reads, the tools it calls, the people who prompt it, and the outputs that reach a client or a court. It sits inside AI security audits and enterprise enablement, so the work is usually done before deployment and repeated as the system changes. Because legal work carries privilege, confidentiality and professional duty, the threat list is wider than a typical software review.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The system under review is usually a hosted model reached through an API, wrapped in a retrieval layer that pulls from a document management system, a contract repository or a matter file. Identity, access control, logging and data residency sit underneath, and most firms run some mix of a public model, a private tenant and a self-hosted option. The threat model has to describe each of these layers, because a weakness in retrieval or permissions often matters more than the model weights. Where a vendor is involved, the review also covers what that vendor retains and for how long.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by mapping the legal workflow, then listing assets such as privileged material, client identifiers and draft advice, and then asking how each could be exposed, altered or fabricated. Common techniques include prompt injection through documents the model reads, data leakage across matters, hallucinated citations, and over-reliance on an output that no lawyer checked. The work borrows from standard threat modelling methods and from red teaming, and it usually produces a written register of threats with owners and mitigations. Findings are tested against real matter data in a sandbox before anything goes live.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The output feeds into firm policy, vendor contracts, insurance review and client terms, and it has to line up with duties of competence, confidentiality and supervision. Records matter here: who approved the tool, what data it may touch, what was logged, and how an incident would be handled.Provenance of outputs, meaning where a claim or citation came from, is part of the control set rather than an afterthought.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect threat modelling to move from a one-off review to a standing control that runs alongside model and vendor changes. Regulatory attention, the volume of AI litigation and the growth of state AI bills all push firms toward documented, repeatable assessments rather than ad hoc sign-off. Agentic tools that take actions rather than only draft text will widen the threat surface, especially around permissions and audit trails. The likely direction is tighter integration between security review, matter intake and client reporting.
